title: Intense flooding slams Florida from a developing storm that could snarl early Thanksgiving travel on the East Coast | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

A rare high risk of flooding is in effect for parts of Florida’s Space Coast through Friday as a dayslong torrential rain event inundates the state’s Atlantic coast, flooding homes and prompting dozens of water rescues.

The relentless downpours are being fueled by a developing storm nearby that could become Tropical or Subtropical Storm Kyle as it heads up the East Coast and disrupts pre-Thanksgiving travel with gusty winds, rain and coastal flooding this weekend.

But first, more flooding rain will fall across a widespread area of Florida from Miami to Jacksonville through Friday.

A number of school districts in Central and South Florida will be closed Friday due to expected weather conditions, including Brevard Public Schools, Broward County Public Schools and the Palm Beach County School District. A couple of additional school districts along Florida’s East Coast have also announced Friday closures, including Flagler Schools and Volusia County Schools.

Florida’s Space Coast faces the most serious, Level 4 of 4 “high” risk of flooding rainfall Thursday and Friday. Up to 10 inches of rain have already fallen in central Brevard County where flash flood warnings were in effect Thursday morning.

High risk flooding days are a big deal: They’re issued on fewer than 4% of days per year on average, but are responsible for more than 80% of all flood-related damage and36% of all flood-related deaths, research from the Weather Prediction Center shows.

More than 100 people were rescued from floodwaters in Brevard County on Thursday, county spokesperson Don Walker told CNN, noting that “countless” homes had water in them.

Roughly 65 homes in the Palm Bay Estates mobile home park in Brevard County were under a mandatory evacuation order Thursday after a bridge washed out and cut off the only access road, Palm Bay Fire Chief Richard Stover told CNN. Residents were evacuated by boat and brought to a temporary shelter, Stover said. The rest of the community is under a voluntary evacuation advisory,according to the city.

Ten people have been evacuated from other areas in Palm Bay as of Thursday afternoon, Stover said. At least two water rescues were conducted, but no injuries have been reported in the city.

The area is still reeling fromhistoric rainfalland severe flooding earlier this month, particularly in Melbourne, which notched its rainiest month on record after seeing over 8 inches of rain this week.

An additional widespread 3 to 6 inches of rain are expected to fall across the Space Coast and northeast Florida through Friday. Totals could soar to 8 to 12 inches or more in new spots.

As of Thursday morning, Daytona Beach has picked up more than four months’ worth of rain — over 13 inches — this week, with more to come.

Rivers still high in the wake of flooding two weeks ago are rising once again. The St. Johns River near Cocoa, Florida, surged past its record-highest crest set more than 70 years ago on Thursday morning.

Wind blowing onshore and high surf are also pounding the Florida coast, producing dangerous rip currents and potentially major beach erosion.

All of this is what’s expected in Florida this fall and winter as thesuper El Niñocontinues to strengthen, changing global weather patterns and increasing storm chances across the US Southeast.

Most forecast models show the storm lifting north along the East Coast this weekend into Monday, but there are still track differences to sort out that will determine exactly where and how impactful it will be to travelers.

There’s a medium chance the storm will transition into a fully tropical or hybrid storm Kyle off the Southeast or Mid-Atlantic coast, but it won’t change the outcome much. Travel will be disrupted during one of the busiest periods of the holiday week, most likely along the Southeast, Mid-Atlantic and New England coasts.

Rainfall, gusty winds and coastal flooding could lash parts northeast Florida and coastal parts of Georgia and the Carolinas as the storm begins to lift north on Saturday or Saturday night. These conditions could cause delays at airports and flood roads, particularly closer to the coast in places from Jacksonville, Florida, to Charleston, South Carolina.

Those impacts could stretch as far north as the Mid-Atlantic and the Northeast, including New York City, on Sunday into Sunday night.

New England will be last to see its blustery downpours before the storm exits the Eastern Seaboard on Monday.

The drenching weather pattern began in South Florida on Tuesday night, with parts of the northern Miami metro area, including Broward County, suffering the worst flooding.

Over a foot of rain — more than three Novembers’ worth — fell in mere hours in the Hollywood area, with some places getting walloped by more than 5 inches of rain per hour, the National Weather Service in Miami said.

Extreme rainfall like this is becomingmore frequent as the world warmsdue to fossil fuel pollution. A warmer atmosphere can soak up more moisture, like a sponge, and wring it out in the form of gushing rainfall.

Broward Countydeclared a state of emergency Wednesday, as did Fort Lauderdaleand Hollywood.

First responders performed water rescues Tuesday night and into Wednesday morning, the Hollywood Police Department told CNN in a statement. The department responded to 64 calls for flood-related assistance between about 3 p.m. and 6 p.m.

The downpour caused the roof to collapse at the Temple Sinai in Hollywood, police said. No injuries were reported.

CNN’s Hanna Park, Jeremy Grisham, Taylor Romine and CNN Meteorologist Mary Gilbert contributed to this report.
